text: Here is a trustworthy saying: whoever aspires to the office of overseer desires a noble task.
An overseer, then, must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach,
not given to drink, not violent, but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money,
managing his own household well, keeping his children obedient with all dignity.

versions.text: managing his own household well, with children who are obedient and entirely respectful.
versions.explanation: μετὰ πάσης σεμνότητος most likely describes the dignified manner in which the overseer governs his household, not a second quality of the children. The revision keeps that ambiguity open and reads more naturally in a series.

text: For if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how can he care for the church of God?
He must not be a recent convert, or he may become conceited and fall under the same judgment as the devil.
He must also have a good reputation with those outside, so that he does not fall into disgrace and into the devil's trap.
Deacons likewise are to be worthy of respect, not double-tongued, not indulging in much wine, not greedy for dishonest gain,
holding the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience.
They too must first be tested; then, if there is nothing against them, let them serve as deacons.
The women likewise are to be worthy of respect, not slanderers, but sober and faithful in everything. [Footnote: Or Their wives; the Greek word can mean either women (deacons) or wives.]

versions.text: The women likewise are to be worthy of respect, not slanderers, but sober and faithful in everything.
versions.explanation: γυναῖκας here is genuinely ambiguous (women serving as deacons, or the wives of deacons). A brief footnote alerts the hearer to the alternative without altering the main text.

text: A deacon must be the husband of one wife, managing his children and his own household well.
For those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves and great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.
I am writing you these things, hoping to come to you soon.
But if I am delayed, you may know how people ought to conduct themselves in God's household, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth.

versions.text: But if I am delayed, you will know how people ought to conduct themselves in God's household, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth.
versions.explanation: The Greek ἵνα εἰδῇς is a purpose clause dependent on "I am writing" in v. 14; the flat indicative "you will know" turns Paul's stated purpose into a prediction. A modal ("you may know") preserves the purpose sense while keeping the sentence readable aloud.

text: Beyond all question, the mystery of godliness is great: He was revealed in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory. [Footnote: Greek Who; some later manuscripts read God.]

versions.text: Beyond all question, the mystery of godliness is great: He was revealed in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.
versions.explanation: The relative pronoun ὅς has no expressed antecedent, and a well-known textual variant reads "God was revealed in the flesh." A short footnote is helpful here and does not disturb the hymn's rhythm.
